title: Pathophysiology: Renal Function—Filtration, Acute Kidney Injury and Chronic Kidney Disease
html:
The kidneys regulate far more than urine volume. They filter plasma, selectively reclaim water and solutes, secrete wastes, concentrate or dilute urine, regulate acid–base balance and blood pressure, activate vitamin D, and produce erythropoietin. Renal dysfunction therefore appears as a pattern involving fluid status, electrolytes, acid–base balance, blood pressure, medication clearance, hematologic and bone health, nutrition, cognition, and cardiovascular risk.

Learning goals

  • Explain filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and excretion across the nephron.
  • Relate renal blood flow, glomerular pressure, and the filtration barrier to GFR.
  • Interpret creatinine, BUN, eGFR, urine output, urinalysis, and trends with appropriate limits.
  • Distinguish prerenal, intrinsic renal, and postrenal mechanisms of acute kidney injury.
  • Compare glomerular, tubular, interstitial, and vascular injury patterns.
  • Explain chronic nephron loss, hyperfiltration, fibrosis, and systemic CKD complications.
  • Recognize urgent hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, severe acidosis, uremia, and obstruction.
  • Connect interventions to perfusion, fluid balance, nephrotoxin exposure, and renal replacement needs.

The nephron filters first, then edits the filtrate

Blood enters the glomerulus through the afferent arteriole and leaves through the efferent arteriole. Hydrostatic pressure drives water and small solutes across the fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte slit barrier into Bowman space. Healthy filtration restricts blood cells and most large proteins.

The tubules then reclaim needed water, electrolytes, glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate and secrete selected acids, potassium, medications, and metabolites. The loop of Henle and medullary concentration gradient help create dilute or concentrated urine. The collecting duct responds to antidiuretic hormone, while aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron.

Excretion = filtration − reabsorption + secretion. A normal urine volume does not prove that filtration or solute clearance is normal, and a low urine volume can reflect decreased perfusion, intrinsic damage, obstruction, hormonal conservation, or collection error.

GFR depends on blood flow, pressure, barrier integrity, and surface area

Glomerular filtration rate reflects the volume of plasma ultrafiltrate formed over time. It depends on renal perfusion, the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic pressures, arteriolar tone, and the permeability and surface area of the filtration barrier. Autoregulation can stabilize renal blood flow and GFR across a range of pressures, but severe or prolonged hypoperfusion overwhelms this protection.

Constriction or dilation of the afferent and efferent arterioles changes pressure within the glomerular capillaries. Neurohormonal responses may preserve filtration temporarily during reduced perfusion, but persistent vasoconstriction can worsen renal oxygen delivery. The renal medulla is especially vulnerable to hypoxic injury because it performs energy-intensive transport in a relatively low-oxygen environment.

Kidney perfusion is not the same as total body fluid
A client can have edema yet reduced effective arterial blood volume and renal perfusion, as in advanced heart failure or cirrhosis. Do not infer that edema automatically means the kidneys are adequately perfused or that additional fluid is safe.

Creatinine and BUN are useful but imperfect signals

Serum creatinine is generated from muscle metabolism and is commonly used to estimate GFR. It may rise only after filtration has already declined, especially early in acute injury. Muscle mass, age, nutrition, amputation, medications, laboratory method, and changing volume status can affect interpretation. A small increase may be important when baseline creatinine is low.

Estimated GFR equations are most useful when kidney function is relatively stable. They are less reliable during rapidly changing acute kidney injury because serum creatinine is not at steady state. Trend the actual creatinine, urine output, fluid balance, exposure history, hemodynamics, urinalysis, and clinical condition.

Blood urea nitrogen is influenced by renal clearance but also by protein intake and breakdown, gastrointestinal bleeding, corticosteroids, liver function, catabolic state, and volume status. The BUN-to-creatinine relationship can support a hypothesis but cannot independently diagnose the mechanism.

Urine and the timeline localize the problem

Accurate urine measurement may reveal declining kidney function before serum markers rise. Confirm collection accuracy, catheter patency when present, recent voiding, intake, losses, and baseline. Oliguria is concerning when persistent or accompanied by worsening perfusion, congestion, potassium, acidosis, or creatinine, but AKI can be nonoliguric.

Urinalysis can reveal protein, blood, leukocytes, glucose, concentration, and sediment findings. Albuminuria suggests glomerular barrier injury and is an important CKD risk marker. Red-cell casts support glomerular inflammation; granular casts may accompany tubular injury; white-cell findings can occur with infection or interstitial inflammation. Findings require the whole clinical context and are not perfectly sensitive or specific.

Ultrasound can help identify hydronephrosis, bladder retention, kidney size, cysts, or structural disease. Normal imaging does not exclude early obstruction or intrinsic kidney injury.

Acute kidney injury is organized by mechanism

AKI is an abrupt decline in kidney function recognized through a rise in creatinine, reduced urine output, or both. Injury categories can overlap and evolve; prolonged prerenal hypoperfusion can progress to intrinsic tubular injury, and obstruction can cause secondary inflammation and damage.

Prerenal: inadequate effective renal perfusion

Mechanisms include volume loss, hemorrhage, vasodilation, shock, low cardiac output, altered renal vascular tone, or reduced effective arterial volume. The kidney initially conserves sodium and water. If perfusion is restored before structural damage, function may improve; indiscriminate fluid administration can be harmful when congestion or pump failure is present.

Intrinsic: injury within vessels, glomeruli, tubules, or interstitium

Ischemia and nephrotoxins can injure tubular epithelial cells, impair reabsorption, promote obstruction by cellular debris, and trigger inflammation. Glomerular inflammation disrupts filtration and may produce hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and edema. Interstitial inflammation may follow medications, infection, or immune processes. Vascular injury can reduce perfusion or damage small vessels.

Postrenal: obstruction to urine flow

Obstruction raises pressure upstream and reduces net filtration. Causes include stones, clots, tumors, strictures, prostatic enlargement, neurogenic bladder, and blocked drainage devices. Bilateral obstruction—or unilateral obstruction in a solitary functioning kidney—can cause substantial AKI. Timely relief may restore function, but rapid decompression requires monitoring for hematuria, hypotension, electrolyte shifts, and post-obstructive diuresis.

Medication and procedure exposures can alter renal function

Risk rises with preexisting CKD, diabetes, older age, sepsis, hypovolemia, heart failure, repeated insults, and multiple nephrotoxic exposures. Potential contributors include selected antimicrobials, contrast exposure, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, calcineurin inhibitors, and combinations that alter renal perfusion. Some medications are directly toxic; others change arteriolar tone or accumulate when clearance falls.

The RN reconciles prescription, over-the-counter, herbal, and recent procedural exposures; reviews indication and renal dosing; monitors ordered levels and renal trends; and promptly communicates new oliguria, rising creatinine, electrolyte change, rash, eosinophilia, or systemic deterioration. Do not independently stop essential therapy unless emergency protocol or scope authorizes it.

Chronic kidney disease is defined by persistence, not one result

CKD reflects abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for at least three months and affecting health. Classification incorporates the cause, GFR category, and albuminuria category. One low eGFR during acute illness does not establish CKD, and a normal-range eGFR does not exclude CKD when persistent albuminuria or structural damage is present.

With progressive nephron loss, remaining nephrons enlarge and hyperfilter to maintain total GFR. This adaptation supports function initially but increases intraglomerular pressure and workload, promoting protein leakage, inflammation, sclerosis, and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Diabetes, hypertension, recurrent injury, smoking, and persistent albuminuria can accelerate progression.

CKD becomes a multisystem disorder

  • Fluid and blood pressure: sodium retention and neurohormonal activation contribute to hypertension, edema, and pulmonary congestion.
  • Potassium and acid–base: reduced potassium and acid excretion can cause hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis.
  • Anemia: reduced erythropoietin, inflammation, iron restriction, blood loss, and shortened red-cell survival can contribute.
  • Mineral and bone disorder: phosphate retention, reduced active vitamin D, hypocalcemic drive, and secondary hyperparathyroidism alter bone and vascular health.
  • Cardiovascular disease: hypertension, volume overload, anemia, inflammation, vascular calcification, and shared risk factors markedly increase cardiovascular risk.
  • Nutrition and neurologic function: anorexia, nausea, pruritus, sleep disturbance, neuropathy, cognitive change, and muscle wasting may develop as toxin burden and systemic illness progress.

Uremia is a clinical syndrome, not simply a high urea value

Uremia results from accumulation of many retained solutes and broader loss of renal regulatory function. Possible manifestations include nausea, anorexia, fatigue, pruritus, altered mentation, asterixis, platelet dysfunction and bleeding, neuropathy, and pericarditis. BUN is a marker, not the only toxic substance or a stand-alone dialysis trigger.

New confusion, seizure, pericardial chest pain or rub, significant bleeding, or severe progressive symptoms in advanced renal failure requires urgent evaluation.

Recognize complications that may require renal replacement

Dialysis or another renal-replacement modality may be needed for severe acid–base disturbance, dangerous electrolyte abnormality, selected dialyzable toxin exposure, fluid overload causing organ compromise, or symptomatic uremia when these problems are refractory to appropriate medical treatment. The decision depends on severity, trajectory, reversibility, overall goals, and specialist evaluation—not a creatinine number alone.

For clients receiving hemodialysis, protect the vascular access, assess for infection and distal perfusion, and follow local policy for blood pressure, venipuncture, and compression. Monitor weight, hemodynamics, symptoms, electrolytes, and access function before and after therapy. Peritoneal dialysis requires strict aseptic technique and assessment of inflow, outflow, abdominal symptoms, respiratory tolerance, and effluent characteristics.

Escalate the dangerous pattern
New ECG changes with hyperkalemia, acute pulmonary edema, severe or worsening acidosis, rapidly declining urine output with instability, suspected obstruction with infection, uremic encephalopathy, pericarditis, or uncontrolled bleeding requires urgent action.

Treatment follows the mechanism and avoids secondary harm

Care may include restoring appropriate perfusion, treating shock or infection, relieving obstruction, removing or adjusting nephrotoxic and renally cleared medications through the authorized team, managing fluid and electrolytes, supporting nutrition, and initiating renal replacement when indicated. Fluid strategy must be individualized: both under-resuscitation and fluid overload can worsen outcomes.

Monitor intake and output, daily weight under consistent conditions, edema, lung sounds, blood pressure, perfusion, mental status, ECG when indicated, creatinine and BUN trends, potassium, bicarbonate, sodium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, glucose, hemoglobin, and medication effects. Compare every result with baseline, timing, and therapy.

Translate renal physiology into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify baseline renal function, urine output and quality, fluid balance, weight, hemodynamics, perfusion, congestion, medications and procedures, infection, obstruction symptoms, urinalysis, electrolytes, acid–base status, and neurologic findings.
  2. Analyze cues: Determine whether the pattern suggests prerenal hypoperfusion, intrinsic glomerular, tubular, interstitial or vascular injury, postrenal obstruction, CKD, or overlapping mechanisms.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Life-threatening hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, severe acidosis, infected obstruction, uremic complications, and shock outrank an isolated stable laboratory change.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan ABC and ECG support, hemodynamic assessment, accurate urine measurement, exposure review, medication safeguards, diagnostic studies, fluid strategy, obstruction relief, and specialist escalation.
  5. Take action: Stabilize the client, verify collection and device patency, implement prescribed treatment, avoid preventable nephrotoxic exposure, and communicate the trend and likely mechanism.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess urine output, perfusion, congestion, weight, symptoms, mentation, ECG, creatinine trajectory, electrolytes, acid–base balance, and adverse effects.

Clinical example

A client with vomiting and diarrhea becomes hypotensive and oliguric. Creatinine is rising, but the lungs remain clear and there is no edema. The RN recognizes possible prerenal AKI from volume loss while also screening for medications, bleeding, sepsis, obstruction, and intrinsic injury. The RN confirms urine measurement, assesses perfusion and losses, escalates the trend, implements the prescribed fluid and diagnostic plan, and reassesses pressure, mentation, urine output, lung findings, creatinine, potassium, and acid–base status. If crackles or hypoxemia develop, the plan is reevaluated rather than continuing fluid automatically.
